correctness.rationale: For two Lanczos steps the approximation lies in span{b,Ab}, hence equals p(A)b for a linear polynomial p. Functional calculus on the symmetric projected 2-by-2 matrix shows that p interpolates the exponential at the two Ritz values. Compression puts those Ritz values in [mu,L]. A mean-value representation of the secant slope gives p(lambda) >= exp(-t theta_1)[1-t(lambda-theta_1)] to the right of the larger Ritz value, proving nonnegativity when t(L-mu)<=1. For t(L-mu)>1, a three-point diagonal spectrum with its middle point approaching mu makes the limiting extrapolated value at L negative; continuity under a positive third starting component converts this into an actual sign failure. Dimension at most two is exact by the minimal-polynomial property. The packaged checker independently verifies the explicit witness.

originality.rationale: The foundational Gallopoulos-Saad report defines the projected exponential approximation, its parabolic motivation, the Lanczos specialization for symmetric matrices, and exactness at the minimal-polynomial dimension. Saad's later analysis supplies the interpolation viewpoint, while later Lanczos papers emphasize convergence and error. Targeted searches did not locate a componentwise positivity theorem with the sharp spectral-width constant one or the dimension-three sharpness mechanism.

value.rationale: Matrix-exponential Krylov propagation is a classical tool for parabolic evolution problems, where nonnegative states such as temperatures or concentrations are natural. The theorem gives a complete, dimension-free positivity guarantee for the first nontrivial Lanczos truncation and proves the constant one sharp. It also identifies a minimal three-mode mechanism showing that excellent spectral conditioning alone does not protect componentwise sign once the time-spectral-width product exceeds one. This is structurally distinct from ordinary norm-error analysis and directly informs the use of very small Krylov dimensions.
